title: Cause and consequence
job: Why things happen and what follows, across a paragraph
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: fa- is a CLITIC of consequence, written joined to the verb it introduces exactly as sa- and li- are: dhahabtu ilā as-sūq, fa-ishtaraytu al-khubz. L1-M9's li-dhālika is its fuller twin and is what opens a fresh sentence; fa- hangs the next clause off the one before it, which is how Arabic runs a paragraph.

Three connectors where English has one "and": wa is mere addition, thumma is mere sequence, fa- is CONSEQUENCE. Choosing fa- is making a claim that the first clause caused the second, so it is never a free substitute for wa.

ammā … fa- is the topic frame: ammā aṭ-ṭaqs fa-kāna bārid. ammā puts a subject up front and the fa- introduces what is said about it. Neither half stands alone — an ammā with no fa- behind it is a sentence cut in two.

bi-sabab (L1-M9) takes a NOUN and only a noun: bi-sabab al-maṭar. li-ʾanna (L1-M9) takes a clause. English hides that split inside one word family — because / because of — so "because we arrived late" has to be nouned: bi-sabab al-wuṣūl mutaʾakhkhiran, L3-M1's maṣdar paying for itself a second time.

li-ʾanna cannot open a sentence. English moves a because-clause to the front whenever it likes; Arabic states the fact and hangs the reason behind it, and a fronted li-ʾanna reads as an answer whose question has gone missing.

li-ʾanna is one of ʾanna's sisters, so the noun behind it is ACCUSATIVE and a pronoun ATTACHES: li-ʾannī, li-ʾannahu, both L1-M9's. li-ʾanna huwa is the shape an English speaker writes and Arabic does not have. This course writes initial hamza, so that ʾanna and L3-M3's anna are two separate entries on the ladder, not one.

mimmā hangs a result on the whole clause before it, and natījatan opens one. yuʾaddī ilā, yusabbib, sabbaba and nātij ʿan are the plainer, more written ways to name the same link — and every one of them joins NOUNS, so a verb has to become a maṣdar before it can stand on either side.

sentences.cue: I went to the market, so I bought the bread

words.note: fa- is a clitic of consequence, written onto the front of its verb like sa- and li-. It says the second thing happened because of the first.

sentences.trap: English's "and" covers wa, thumma and fa- alike. Only fa- claims the first clause caused the second, so where English chooses nothing Arabic is choosing.
sentences.sound: fash-ta-RAY-tu, with no pause after the fa-: it is a letter riding on the verb, never a word standing beside it.

variations.cue: I went to the market, so I bought the water
variations.changed: what was bought: al-khubz → al-māʾ

variations.display: dhahabtu ilā as-sūq, wa ishtaraytu al-khubz
variations.cue: I went to the market and bought the bread
variations.changed: the connector: fa- → wa, and the causal claim goes with it

mistake.display: dhahabtu ilā as-sūq, wa fa-ishtaraytu al-khubz
mistake.why: wa and fa- are both connectors and only one of them may hold that slot. fa- replaces wa; it never queues up behind it.

sentences.usage: The everyday way to tell a short account of what you did: one clause, and the next hung straight off it.
sentences.mnemonic: fa- is the "so" you can lean a whole paragraph on.

sentences.cue: The manager is angry, so he is going home

words.note: fa- takes a person the way L1-M6's sa- did: fa-adhhab I, fa-tadhhab you, fa-yadhhab he. The clitic never changes; only the verb under it does.

sentences.trap: English can drop the second subject — "he is angry, so going home". Arabic cannot: the person lives in the verb, and fa- attaches to a verb that already carries it.
sentences.sound: fa-YADH-hab: one word, stress on the stem, and the fa- said so lightly it is easy to miss when listening.

variations.cue: I'm angry, so I'm going home
variations.changed: the person: he → I, and the verb cell with it

variations.cue: The manager is angry, so he is going to work
variations.changed: where he goes: al-bayt → al-ʿamal

mistake.display: al-mudīr ghāḍib, fa yadhhab ilā al-bayt
mistake.script: المدير غاضب، ف يذهب إلى البيت
mistake.why: fa- is never a word on its own — it is a single letter joined to what follows, which is why this course hyphenates it. Standing apart it is not Arabic.

sentences.usage: Reporting somebody else's reaction: the state, then what it makes them do.
sentences.mnemonic: One letter, three persons — the verb does the changing.

sentences.display: lā adhhab ilā al-ʿamal bi-sabab al-maṭar
sentences.script: لا أذهب إلى العمل بسبب المطر
sentences.cue: I'm not going to work because of the rain
sentences.literal: Not I-go to the-work because-of the-rain

words.note: The rain as a thing, which is exactly what bi-sabab needs. bi-sabab is L1-M9's and holds a noun; li-ʾanna, also L1-M9's, holds a whole clause.

sentences.trap: English's "because" and "because of" look like one word with a tail on it. Arabic splits them into two unrelated frames: li-ʾanna takes a clause, bi-sabab takes a bare noun and nothing else.
sentences.sound: bi-SA-bab al-ma-ṬAR — bi- is a clitic like fa-, so it leans on sabab and takes no pause.

variations.display: lā adhhab ilā as-sūq bi-sabab al-maṭar
variations.script: لا أذهب إلى السوق بسبب المطر
variations.cue: I'm not going to the market because of the rain
variations.changed: the destination: al-ʿamal → as-sūq

variations.display: lā adhhab ilā al-ʿamal bi-sabab al-izdiḥām
variations.script: لا أذهب إلى العمل بسبب الازدحام
variations.cue: I'm not going to work because of the traffic
variations.changed: the cause: al-maṭar → al-izdiḥām

mistake.display: lā adhhab ilā al-ʿamal bi-sabab al-maṭar shadīd
mistake.script: لا أذهب إلى العمل بسبب المطر شديد
mistake.why: A clause has been pushed in behind bi-sabab, which only holds a noun. Either stop at the noun, or switch frames: li-ʾanna al-maṭar shadīd.

sentences.usage: The commonest excuse shape there is — a reason given as a thing rather than as a story.
sentences.mnemonic: bi-sabab wants a thing; li-ʾanna wants a sentence.

sentences.cue: I arrived late because of the traffic

words.note: The -an tail of an adverb, as on L3-M1's dāʾiman. The ʾ inside it is hamza, the catch in the throat, and never the ʿayn of ʿamal.
Literally the crowding — a maṣdar doing duty as an everyday noun. It is the word for traffic on a road.

sentences.trap: To say "because we arrived late", bi-sabab cannot hold the clause. The arriving has to become a noun first: bi-sabab al-wuṣūl mutaʾakhkhiran, which is L3-M1's maṣdar earning its keep a second time.
sentences.sound: mu-ta-ʾAKH-khi-ran — five syllables, the kh doubled and held, and the -an clipped short at the end.

variations.cue: I arrived late because of the rain
variations.changed: the cause: al-izdiḥām → al-maṭar

variations.display: kāna al-mudīr ghāḍib bi-sabab al-wuṣūl mutaʾakhkhiran
variations.script: كان المدير غاضب بسبب الوصول متأخرًا
variations.cue: The manager was angry because of the late arrival
variations.changed: the clause behind bi-sabab, nouned into a maṣdar

mistake.why: A finite verb parked behind bi-sabab. It holds nouns only, so the verb has to turn into its maṣdar: bi-sabab al-wuṣūl.

sentences.usage: Arriving anywhere late, in an office or a message: the fact first, then the thing that caused it.
sentences.mnemonic: If a verb has to follow bi-sabab, it stops being a verb first.

sentences.cue: Lateness is a problem, so I go early

words.note: The maṣdar standing behind mutaʾakhkhiran. t is a sun letter, so the article is heard as at-, and the ʾ inside is hamza.

sentences.trap: li-dhālika is the twin of fa-, not a synonym of it. It opens a new sentence and takes a full clause after it; fa- rides on a verb and cannot start anything.
sentences.sound: at-ta-ʾAKH-khur — the same doubled, held kh as mutaʾakhkhiran, because it is the same root standing still.

variations.cue: Traffic is a problem, so I go early
variations.changed: the problem named: at-taʾakhkhur → al-izdiḥām

variations.cue: Lateness is a problem, so I'm not going
variations.changed: the consequence: going early → not going

mistake.why: Both consequence markers at once. Pick one: fa- attached to the verb, or li-dhālika opening the clause — stacking them says the same thing twice.

sentences.usage: Stating a policy or a habit and the reasoning behind it, in the order Arabic prefers: fact, then consequence.
sentences.mnemonic: fa- rides a verb; li-dhālika opens a sentence.

words.note: "Leads to", and it will not go without its ilā. Both ends of it are nouns, so a verb standing on either side has to become a maṣdar first.

sentences.trap: English lets a whole clause follow "leads to" — leads to us being late. yuʾaddī ilā takes a noun on both sides, which is why this course spent L3-M1 on the maṣdar.
sentences.sound: yu-ʾAD-dī: the ʾ is hamza on the seat of a w, the d is doubled and held, and the final ī is long.

variations.cue: Rain leads to traffic
variations.changed: both ends of the link: rain causes the crowding

variations.cue: Traffic causes delay
variations.changed: the verb: yuʾaddī ilā → yusabbib, which needs no preposition

mistake.why: The ilā has gone, and without it yuʾaddī means something else entirely — performing a task, not leading to a result. The preposition is part of the meaning.

sentences.usage: The written, explaining register: reports, notices, an argument being laid out rather than a story being told.
sentences.mnemonic: yuʾaddī always arrives with ilā in its hand.

sentences.cue: As for the weather, it was cold

words.note: Puts a topic up front. It cannot stand alone: whatever is said about that topic must begin with fa-, so ammā and fa- always arrive as a pair.
ṭ is a sun letter, so the article's l is swallowed: al-ṭaqs is said and written aṭ-ṭaqs. The ṭ is the emphatic one, tongue flat.
The second half of the ammā frame. Here fa- is not consequence but the answer to a topic — the same letter doing the frame's other job.

sentences.trap: English's "as for X" is optional decoration you can drop at will. ammā is structural: once it has been said the sentence cannot finish without fa-, and leaving it out sounds like a line cut in half.
sentences.sound: AM-mā with the m held, then fa-KĀ-na run together — the fa- never takes a pause, even at the seam of the frame.

variations.cue: As for the manager, he was angry
variations.changed: the topic: the weather → the manager

variations.cue: The weather is cold
variations.changed: the frame dropped, leaving the bare statement

mistake.why: The fa- is missing, and with it the second half of the frame. ammā announces a topic and fa- is what answers it — one without the other is not a sentence.

sentences.usage: Turning to a new subject inside a longer account: after the journey, the food, then "as for the weather…".
sentences.mnemonic: ammā opens a door that only fa- can close.

sentences.display: waṣala al-mudīr mutaʾakhkhiran, mimmā sabbaba mushkila
sentences.script: وصل المدير متأخرًا، مما سبب مشكلة
sentences.cue: The manager arrived late, which caused a problem
sentences.literal: Arrived the-manager late, which caused problem

words.note: Hangs a consequence on the whole clause before it, not on any one word of it. It is min plus mā run together into one word.
Past tense, "caused". It takes its result as a bare object with no preposition — unlike yuʾaddī, which needs its ilā.

sentences.trap: English's "which" can point at a noun or at a whole clause. Arabic splits the job: alladhī points at a noun, mimmā points at everything just said.
sentences.sound: MIM-mā — the m doubled and held, which is the whole audible difference between it and min mā said slowly.

variations.cue: I arrived late, which caused a problem
variations.changed: who arrived: the manager → I

variations.display: waṣala al-mudīr mutaʾakhkhiran, wa hādhā sabbaba mushkila
variations.script: وصل المدير متأخرًا، وهذا سبب مشكلة
variations.cue: The manager arrived late, and this caused a problem
variations.changed: the link: mimmā → wa hādhā, the plainer spoken version

mistake.display: waṣala al-mudīr mutaʾakhkhiran, alladhī sabbaba mushkila
mistake.script: وصل المدير متأخرًا، الذي سبب مشكلة
mistake.why: alladhī has to attach to a noun, and here it would attach to the manager — as though he were the problem. Pointing at the whole clause is mimmā's job.

sentences.usage: Written and careful speech: a report, a complaint, an account where the consequence is of the situation and not of one person.
sentences.mnemonic: mimmā points backwards at everything you just said.

sentences.cue: The delay results from the traffic

words.note: Not a verb but a describing word, "resulting". It needs ʿan behind it: nātij ʿan is "arising out of".
Thirty modules and the ladder had never bought it. Here it is "out of"; its other everyday job is "about", as in speaking about a thing.

sentences.trap: This says the same thing as bi-sabab, backwards: bi-sabab hangs the cause on the result, nātij ʿan hangs the result on the cause. English's "because of" only goes one way.
sentences.sound: NĀ-tij ʿan — the ʿ of ʿan is the throat-squeeze of L1-M4's ʿamal, and it swallows the pause between the two words.

variations.cue: The traffic results from the rain
variations.changed: both ends: the crowding is now the result

variations.cue: The delay results from the rain
variations.changed: the cause: al-izdiḥām → al-maṭar

mistake.why: min is the ordinary "from" of places and materials. nātij takes ʿan, and the pairing is fixed — the word carries its preposition with it.

sentences.usage: Announcements and written notices, where the cause is stated as a fact about the result rather than as an excuse.

sentences.display: al-maṭar yusabbib al-izdiḥām, wa natījatan waṣaltu mutaʾakhkhiran
sentences.script: المطر يسبب الازدحام، ونتيجةً وصلت متأخرًا
sentences.cue: Rain causes traffic, and as a result I arrived late
sentences.literal: The-rain causes the-crowding, and as-a-result I-arrived late

words.note: The present of sabbaba. Written without a final -u because this course writes no mood endings, exactly as it writes adhhab and yadhhab.
"As a result", opening the clause it belongs to. The -an tail is the adverb ending of L3-M1's dāʾiman and this level's mutaʾakhkhiran.

sentences.trap: English can end on "as a result" — I was late as a result. natījatan opens its clause and stays at the front, the way awwalan and akhīran do.
sentences.sound: na-tī-ja-tan: the feminine ending is heard as -tan here, not -a, because the adverbial -an is sitting on it.

variations.display: al-maṭar yusabbib al-izdiḥām, wa natījatan lā adhhab
variations.script: المطر يسبب الازدحام، ونتيجةً لا أذهب
variations.cue: Rain causes traffic, and as a result I'm not going
variations.changed: the result clause: arriving late → not going

variations.display: al-izdiḥām yusabbib at-taʾakhkhur, wa natījatan waṣaltu mutaʾakhkhiran
variations.script: الازدحام يسبب التأخر، ونتيجةً وصلت متأخرًا
variations.cue: Traffic causes delay, and as a result I arrived late
variations.changed: the first clause: the cause moves one link down the chain

mistake.display: al-maṭar yusabbib al-izdiḥām, waṣaltu mutaʾakhkhiran natījatan
mistake.script: المطر يسبب الازدحام، وصلت متأخرًا نتيجةً
mistake.why: natījatan has been left at the end, English-fashion. It is a clause opener: it goes in front of the result, not behind it.

sentences.usage: The last link of a chain of causes — the one that says how the whole thing landed on you.
sentences.mnemonic: natījatan leads its clause; it never trails one.

The manager is angry, so he is going home

comprehensionPool.script: لا أذهب إلى العمل بسبب المطر
comprehensionPool.cue: I'm not going to work because of the rain
I arrived late because of the traffic
Lateness is a problem, so I go early
As for the weather, it was cold

comprehensionPool.cue: The manager arrived late, which caused a problem

comprehensionPool.display: aṭ-ṭaqs bārid al-yawm, li-dhālika lā adhhab
comprehensionPool.script: الطقس بارد اليوم، لذلك لا أذهب
comprehensionPool.cue: The weather is cold today, so I'm not going
As for the manager, he was angry
